## 2. How to run it

Everything is already installed and configured. Node is managed by nvm.

```bash
# interactive terminals pick this up from ~/.zshrc automatically.
# a non-interactive shell (like an agent's Bash tool) does NOT, so prefix with:
export NVM_DIR="$HOME/.nvm"; . /opt/homebrew/opt/nvm/nvm.sh; nvm use 22
export COREPACK_ENABLE_DOWNLOAD_PROMPT=0
```

Toolchain: Node 22.23.2 (nvm), Yarn 3.2.1 (via corepack), Docker 28.4.0, gh 2.100.0 (authed as angrapsas).
Do NOT use Node 24 — some suites fail on it. Homebrew also has a Node 26 that nvm shadows.

### Two separate apps

**A. The monorepo** at `~/medusa` — the actual Medusa source, what we make PRs against.

```bash
cd ~/medusa
yarn install                                    # ~1 min
yarn build                                      # ~2.5 min, 80 packages
yarn workspace @medusajs/dashboard dev          # admin dashboard dev server on :5173
yarn workspace @medusajs/ui storybook           # design system on :6006
```

**B. A scaffolded store** at `~/my-store` — created with create-medusa-app, used to click around a
real running store. Uses PUBLISHED medusa packages from npm, NOT the local source, so changes to
`~/medusa` do NOT show up here.

```bash
docker start medusa-postgres                    # postgres:15 on :5433, db `my_store`, postgres/postgres
cd ~/my-store/apps/backend && npm run dev       # admin at :9000/app
```

Admin login exists (created during Sprint 0). Store is seeded: 4 products, 20 variants, 2 orders,
1 region (Europe/EUR), 1 sales channel.

**Which one to use:** :5173 to see your own dashboard changes. :9000 to see a fully working store
with data. They are different codebases.

**Running my local code end to end (used for the Lightning Talk screenshots, Oct 19):**

## 3. Known broken things (all upstream Medusa, not our fork)

Our fork only adds STUDENTS.md and course files on top of Medusa 2.17.2. These are real upstream bugs.

**1. 467 unit tests fail on a clean checkout.** `@medusajs/icons` 464/464 and `@medusajs/ui` 3/40.
All from one cause: `packages/design-system/icons/package.json` declares
`react: "^18.3.1 || ^19.0.0"` in devDependencies, so Yarn nests react@19.2.6 inside that package
while `react-dom@18.3.1` stays hoisted at root. React 19 elements + React 18 renderer =
"Objects are not valid as a React child". Fix: scoped resolution `"@medusajs/icons/react": "^18.3.1"`
in root package.json — precedent already exists there for `@redocly/cli/react`.
**68 of 70 packages pass.** Confirmed by three of us independently. NOT your machine.

**2. The standalone dashboard dev server renders a blank page.**
`packages/admin/dashboard/vite.config.mts` defines only 3 of the 6 globals the source needs.
Missing: `__AUTH_TYPE__`, `__JWT_TOKEN_STORAGE_KEY__`, `__MAX_UPLOAD_FILE_SIZE__`.
`src/lib/client/client.ts:3` throws a ReferenceError before React mounts. The bundled admin at
:9000 works because `admin-bundler/src/utils/config.ts:52-57` defines all six. Config was last
touched 2024-10-09; the source added those globals in late 2025. Nobody has fixed it.
Workaround already in the repo: `vi.hoisted()` in three spec files sets the globals for tests.

**3. Form validation errors never display anywhere in the dashboard.**
`@hookform/resolvers@3.4.2` with `zod@4.2.0`. Resolvers v3 doesn't understand zod 4 errors, so
instead of putting them in form state it throws. **116 files use zodResolver, 104 render
`<Form.ErrorMessage />`, and none of them can show anything.** Submitting an invalid form just
silently refuses. Verified by running validation directly: errors exist with messages, they just
never reach the form.

**#58 in one paragraph (I get asked about this):** completing a cart when an item sold out returned
a 400 with no cart, so the storefront could not show which item was the problem. The error comes
from `ensureInventoryLevels` in the inventory module, thrown as `NOT_ALLOWED`. The promotion-limit
and subscription errors from the same workflow are also `NOT_ALLOWED`, so the route could not branch
on type. I attached the existing `INSUFFICIENT_INVENTORY` code to the error at its source and added
a `statusOKErrorCodes` list to `packages/medusa/src/api/store/carts/[id]/complete/route.ts`.
Rejected alternatives: allow the whole `NOT_ALLOWED` type (swallows the other two), pre-check stock
(extra query on every checkout and still racy), new error type (the HTTP error handler does not know
it, so other routes 500). Cost: handled errors now live in two lists, and the code appears in other
routes' error bodies, which required updating two reservation tests.

The team's second tech showcase was **Ponytail** (https://ponytail.dev,
github.com/DietrichGebert/ponytail, MIT), a Claude Code plugin that injects a decision ladder
(stdlib → native platform feature → reuse existing project code → only then write new code) so the
agent stops over-engineering. Published benchmarks: 54% less code, 27% faster, 20% lower API cost,
with validation and security never simplified away. Commands: `/ponytail-review` (scan the current

## 9. Lessons learned

Medusa core is deliberately minimal; the plugin ecosystem fills feature gaps. **Before proposing
anything, search externally, not just the repo.** Ideas that looked like gaps but already exist as
official or community plugins: Shopify migration (Medusa's own MCP server does it), sales analytics
dashboard (Agilo and rsc-labs plugins), abandoned cart recovery (community plugin + Medusa guide).

The proposals that survive are ones a plugin **cannot** add — engine behavior, admin API routes,
core defaults. That's why #16 and #23 hold up.

Also verified as genuinely missing: order CSV import (products have import+export, orders have
export only), customer export, and **a count of how many times a product has sold** —
`order_line_item` has indexed `product_id` and `variant_id` plus `quantity`, so the data is there
and indexed; nobody surfaced it. That last one is a natural sequel to #9 (order count + lifetime
spend for customers, which lefecko already merged).

From Sprint 1:
- **Read the code before trusting an issue's scope.** #32 already existed, #16 was smaller than written.
- **Claim issues and get spec review comments at the start of the sprint.** Sprint 1 all landed on the last day.
- **Never paste issue/PR text copied from the terminal.** It mangled #32 and #40 twice. Save to a file and
  post with `gh issue edit N --body-file <file>` / `gh pr create --body-file <file>`.
- **Run parallel work in separate git worktrees**: `git worktree add ~/medusa-<n> -b <branch> origin/develop`.
- **Watch AI scope creep.** On #11 it added a whole-number rule for weights nobody asked for. Tell it to stick to
  the acceptance criteria and check commit messages before every commit.

From Sprint 2:
- **Sprint 0 lost D4/D5 points because no issue comment linked the logs.** The link has to open the
  log file itself, not the folder. One "AI Assistance" comment per contributor per issue.
- **The error you are looking for is often not where the obvious code is.** On #58 I assumed
  `confirm-inventory.ts` because it already used `INSUFFICIENT_INVENTORY`. That step does not run on
  cart completion at all. Trace the real path before designing.
- **Tag an error at its source, match on the tag at the boundary.** Beats pattern-matching messages
  or widening a type list that other errors share.
- **Every PR needs the Tech Debt section**, split into Introduced (a tradeoff you chose) and
  Encountered (pre-existing, scoped out). Sprint 3 adds Test Evidence on top of it.
- **Reviews must be substantive.** On #89 I checked out the branch, ran it, and reverted the author's
  fix to confirm his new test actually failed. That is the kind of thing worth writing down in the
  review.
- **Diagrams need a legend and annotations or they lose points**, even when the structure is right.

## 11. Conventions to follow

- Prettier: no semicolons, double quotes, 2-space indent, ES5 trailing commas. `npx prettier --check <files>`
- Files kebab-case, types PascalCase, functions camelCase, constants SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE, DB fields snake_case
- Commit style is mixed on the team: conventional (`feat(dashboard): ...`) and plain imperative both appear
- **Changesets required** — add one as a separate `chore:` commit. See `.changeset/` for format
- PR description format: What / Why / How / Testing, in plain prose, first person. Include the
  command to run the tests. No checklists, no bolded headers — teammates don't use them
- `Co-Authored-By: Claude ...` trailers appear on some commits (lefecko uses them, upstream Medusa
  does too). Not required
- AI logs go to `ai-logs/sprint<N>/<username>/YYYY-MM-DD_<tool>_<short-slug>.md`. Link the log from
  the issue or PR it documents, as a full URL that opens the file itself, not the folder
- My commits: short plain subject only ("Add ...", "Fix ..."), no body, no Co-Authored-By line
- Every PR gets a teammate review with the course rubric. **Never self-approve or self-merge**

**New in Sprint 3 (see `sprint3.md` for the full text):**
- Every PR description needs a **Test Evidence** table (one row per AC: test, level, source of the
  expected value) on top of the Tech Debt section. The source of an expected value may never be
  "what the code currently returns"
- A PR merges only after a teammate approves **the latest commit**. Pushing after an approval
  invalidates it
- A **spec review comment on the issue, before coding**, that states what the reviewer checked
- Use `Closes #<issue>` in the PR description and attach issues and PRs to the sprint milestone
- D6 mutation testing uses **StrykerJS** (Jest runner for backend packages, Vitest runner for the
  dashboard), run only on the files the PR changed, with before/after JSON reports committed

## 12. How I like to work

- Find the code myself first, then use AI to check my understanding. The course grades this

- Verify claims by running things, don't assert from reading. Prove a test fails without the fix
- Don't post to GitHub (issues, PRs, comments, reviews, tags) without showing me the exact text first
- Keep writing plain. No em dashes, no AI-sounding scaffolding. Match my teammates' register

### D5 - AI Logs (5 pts, individual)

Same requirements as Sprint 1 and the AI Log Instructions, with the enforcement in item 5 above.

**Log storage:** `ai-logs/sprint3/angrapsas/`

### D6 - Mutation Testing (15 pts, individual) - NEW

**What it is.** A mutation testing tool makes small changes to your code (**mutants**), such as
flipping a condition or changing a boundary value, and runs your tests against each one. If a test
fails, the mutant is **killed**. If all tests pass, the mutant **survived**: your tests did not
notice that the code changed. Survivors point to weak or missing tests.

**What to do.** For one of your issues whose PR changes source code and tests
(**CSCI 535: two such issues**; your small issue may be one of them):

1. Run a mutation testing tool **on the source files changed by your PR(s) for that issue**. Do not
   run it on the whole project.
2. Using the tool's report, **analyze every surviving mutant**: is it **equivalent** (it behaves
   exactly like the original code, so no test can kill it), or does it reveal a **gap** in your
   tests? If there are more than 10 survivors, analyze at least 10, starting with those in lines
   your PR added or changed.
3. **Add or strengthen at least one test that kills a surviving mutant** that revealed a gap.
   Re-run the tool to confirm it is killed. If no survivor reveals a gap (all killed or equivalent),
   say so and justify it in the surviving-mutants table; that completes this step.
4. Answer the questions in the template.

**Evidence.** Configure the tool to write a machine-readable report (**StrykerJS: add `"json"` to
`reporters`**). Commit the report from the first run and the re-run as
`docs/sprint3/mutation/reports/<issue#>-<username>-before.json` and `-after.json`. The mutation
scores you list must match the reports, and the mutant your new test kills must show as killed in
the "after" report.

**A tool is required. Manual mutation does not count.**

| Stack | Tool |
|---|---|
| **TypeScript/JavaScript with Jest (Medusa)** | **StrykerJS with the Jest runner** |
| TypeScript/JavaScript with Vitest | StrykerJS with the Vitest runner |
| Go | Gremlins or go-mutesting |

**Note for us:** Medusa is mixed. Backend packages use **Jest**, the dashboard uses **Vitest**.
Pick the runner that matches the files the PR changed.

**Set it up early.** Getting the tool to work on a large codebase is real work: builds, services,
choosing which tests run. Each student configures and runs the tool for their own files and commits
the configuration used. **You may reuse a teammate's setup (and are encouraged to)**, as long as you
run the tool yourself and credit the teammate in your report.

**Common problems to watch for:**
- **The tool stops before mutating.** Tools first run your tests on the unchanged code. If any
  selected test fails, the run stops. Fix or exclude failing tests first (this is where the baseline
  run helps). *Relevant to us: see HANDOFF section 3 and issue #98.*
- **Tests run against built code.** If tests run against compiled output (a `dist` folder) instead
  of the source, mutants in the source are never seen. Configure the tool to rebuild before testing,
  or choose tests that run on source. *Relevant to us: the integration tests load `dist`.*
- **Tests need services.** Some suites need a database or another service running. Start them first.
- **False survivors.** If you limit which tests run, make sure the tests that cover the mutated
  files are included. Otherwise mutants some test would catch are reported as survived or not
  covered. Before writing a new test for a survivor, check that the relevant tests actually ran.
- **Long runs.** Mutating only the files changed by the PR keeps run time manageable.

**If you are blocked:** ask teammates first, someone may have a working setup. Still stuck, tell the
TA **as early as possible**, with the errors and the AI log of what you tried. The TA may approve
running the tool on a different issue or part of the code. **Problems reported at the end of the
sprint will not excuse a missing D6.**

```text
// Stryker buildCommand for issue #62 mutation testing.
// Babel, which Stryker uses to instrument the file, drops parameter decorators
// on parameters that have a default value, so every `@MedusaContext() context:
// Context = {}` loses its decorator and @EmitEvents fails at runtime. This puts
// them back before building dist/, which the module tests load.
const fs = require("fs")
const { execSync } = require("child_process")

const file = "src/services/inventory-module.ts"
const pattern = /(?<!@MedusaContext\(\) )\bcontext: Context = \{\}/g

const source = fs.readFileSync(file, "utf8")
const restored = (source.match(pattern) ?? []).length
fs.writeFileSync(
  file,
  source.replace(pattern, "@MedusaContext() context: Context = {}")
)
console.log(`stryker-build: restored ${restored} @MedusaContext() decorators`)

execSync("yarn build", { stdio: "inherit" })
=============== stryker.config.mjs
// Shared Stryker mutation-testing config for the Medusa monorepo.
//
// Setup: Stryker is NOT a committed dependency (it is not in package.json), to
// keep the lockfile untouched. Install it locally without saving it:
//
//   npm install --no-save @stryker-mutator/core@10 @stryker-mutator/jest-runner@10
//
// (or `yarn add -D` the same two packages if you want it in package.json).
// Also build the workspace packages the tests import first, e.g.
//   yarn turbo run build --filter=@medusajs/framework...
//
// Usage: run from INSIDE the package you want to mutate, so Stryker picks up
// that package's own jest.config.js (each package has its own moduleNameMapper
// and transform settings), pointing at this shared file. Call the binary
// directly (`yarn stryker` is not resolvable from a package directory):
//
//   cd packages/core/core-flows
//   node ../../../node_modules/.bin/stryker run ../../../stryker.config.mjs \
//     --mutate "src/product/utils/bundle.ts"
//
// To write the JSON report somewhere specific (the CLI cannot override nested
// options), set STRYKER_JSON_REPORT, e.g.
//   STRYKER_JSON_REPORT=../../../docs/sprint3/mutation/reports/112-lefecko-before.json
//
// Do not run this from the repo root: the root jest.config.js fans out to
// every package as a multi-project config, which would mean mutating (and
// re-testing) the entire monorepo.

/** @type {import("@stryker-mutator/api/core").PartialStrykerOptions} */
export default {
  testRunner: "jest",

  jest: {
    // Use the jest.config.js found in the current working directory (the package).
    configFile: "jest.config.js",
    // Stryker's default injects its own config; keeping this enabled lets it
    // wrap the package config and run tests per mutant.
    enableFindRelatedTests: true,
  },

  // Only mutate source code; skip tests, type declarations, and barrel files.
  mutate: [
    "src/**/*.ts",
    "!src/**/__tests__/**",
    "!src/**/__mocks__/**",
    "!src/**/*.spec.ts",
    "!src/**/*.test.ts",
    "!src/**/*.d.ts",
    "!src/**/index.ts",
    "!src/migrations/**",
  ],

  // "perTest" coverage runs only the tests that touch each mutant, which is a
  // large speedup. Jest supports it natively.
  coverageAnalysis: "perTest",

  // "json" writes the machine-readable report required as D6 evidence. The
  // default path below is a scratch location; for the graded runs, set
  // STRYKER_JSON_REPORT (the CLI cannot override nested options) so the file
  // lands in the committed reports folder, e.g.:
  //   STRYKER_JSON_REPORT=../../../docs/sprint3/mutation/reports/112-lefecko-before.json
  reporters: ["clear-text", "progress", "html", "json"],
  htmlReporter: { fileName: "reports/mutation/index.html" },
  jsonReporter: {
    fileName:
      process.env.STRYKER_JSON_REPORT ?? "reports/mutation/mutation.json",
  },

  // Run mutants directly in the package instead of in a copied sandbox.
  // Package jest configs use relative requires such as
  // require("../../../define_jest_config"); a sandbox under
  // <package>/.stryker-tmp/sandbox-xxx is two directories deeper, so that
  // require fails. inPlace avoids the problem; Stryker restores the original
  // files when the run ends, so commit or stash work first in case a run is
  // killed midway (then `git checkout -- .` restores any leftover mutation).
  inPlace: true,

  // Scratch dir for Stryker's backups/state, placed at the repo root (relative
  // to the package cwd) so Jest does not discover the backup copy of the
  // package's tests inside the package and run every test twice. Ignored by git.
  tempDirName: "../../../.stryker-tmp",

  // Thresholds are informational for now (break: null never fails the run).
  thresholds: { high: 80, low: 60, break: null },

  // Mutation runs are CPU heavy; keep parallelism modest on laptops.
  concurrency: 2,
  timeoutMS: 60000,
}
```

```text
=== 62-njpiombino.md ===
# Mutation testing: Issue #62 -- Add a Low-Stock Inventory Monitoring Dashboard

**PR(s):** [#115](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/medusa/pull/115)  **Tool:** StrykerJS 10.1.1 with the Jest runner (`@stryker-mutator/core`, `@stryker-mutator/jest-runner`)  **Config:** [stryker.config.json](../../../packages/modules/inventory/stryker.config.json) and its build step [stryker-build.cjs](../../../packages/modules/inventory/stryker-build.cjs) (my own setup; no teammate setup existed)  **Command:** `cd packages/modules/inventory && npx stryker run` (Postgres running)
**Reports:** [before](reports/62-njpiombino-before.json) · [after](reports/62-njpiombino-after.json)
**Mutation score:** before 77.78% (56 of 72 killed) → after 84.72% (61 of 72 killed)

**Scope.** Mutated: the 111 lines that #62 added to `packages/modules/inventory/src/services/inventory-module.ts` (lines 443-553: the `stock_status` handling in `listInventoryItems` / `listAndCountInventoryItems` and the SQL helper `listIdsByStockStatus_`). That is where all of the PR's filtering, sorting and paging logic lives. Not mutated:
- the type files, which have no runtime code;
- `validators.ts`, a two-value zod enum covered only by the HTTP suite, which boots a full server against built packages;
- the dashboard files, which are tested with Vitest, not Jest.

Tests run: `packages/modules/inventory/integration-tests/__tests__/inventory-module-service.spec.ts` (44 tests before, 48 after).

**Setup problems solved:**
- The module tests load `dist/`, not `src/`. The config therefore rebuilds the package after Stryker instruments the file (`buildCommand`), and runs `inPlace` because the sandbox copy breaks the package tsconfig's relative `extends`.
- Babel, which Stryker uses to instrument the file, drops parameter decorators on parameters with a default value. Every `@MedusaContext() context: Context = {}` lost its decorator, so 8 existing tests failed in the initial run. This happens in both Babel 8 (Stryker 10) and Babel 7.29 (Stryker 9). `stryker-build.cjs` restores the 35 decorators before building.
- `moduleIntegrationTestRunner` wraps suites in `describe("")`, so Stryker's per-test coverage IDs never match Jest's test names, and every mutant was reported as uncovered. `coverageAnalysis` is set to `all`, so every test runs against every mutant.
- `concurrency` is 1 because every test run uses the same test database name.

## Surviving mutants

All 16 mutants that were not killed in the before run (13 survived, 3 had no coverage). Line numbers are in `packages/modules/inventory/src/services/inventory-module.ts`. The source file is identical in both reports.

| Location (file:line) | Mutation | Equivalent or test gap? | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| inventory-module.ts:450 (#3) | `!filters.stock_status` → `false` in `listInventoryItems` | Equivalent | `listInventoryItems` then always calls `listAndCountInventoryItems`, which runs the same check and returns the same items without the filter. Only an extra count query is added. |
| inventory-module.ts:450 (#4) | early-return block → `{}` | Equivalent | Falls through to the same `listAndCountInventoryItems` path as #3. |
| inventory-module.ts:476 (#12) | `!sortedIds.length` → `false` | Equivalent | With no ids, the intersection query gets `id: []`, which matches nothing, so the result is still `[[], 0]`. The early return only saves two queries. |
| inventory-module.ts:476 (#13) | early-return block → `{}` | Equivalent (no coverage before, survived after) | Same reasoning as #12: falling through produces `[[], 0]`. |
| inventory-module.ts:477 (#14) | `return [[], 0]` → `return []` | Test gap, **killed after** | No test had zero items with the status in the database, so the early return never ran. A caller destructuring `[items, count]` would get `undefined`. |
| inventory-module.ts:477 (#15) | `[]` → `["Stryker was here"]` | Test gap, **killed after** | Same gap as #14: would return a fake item. |
| inventory-module.ts:482 (#18) | `{ id: sortedIds }` → `{}` in the intersection query | Equivalent | The next line filters to `sortedIds` again in memory, so narrowing in SQL only reduces rows read. |
| inventory-module.ts:483 (#19) | `{ select: ["id"] }` → `{}` | Equivalent | Only `id` is read from the result. Selecting all fields gives the same ids. |
| inventory-module.ts:483 (#20) | `["id"]` → `[]` | Equivalent | An empty select loads default fields, which include `id`. |
| inventory-module.ts:483 (#21) | `"id"` → `""` | Equivalent | The query still returns the primary key, the only field used. |
| inventory-module.ts:492 (#27) | `config.take == null` → `true` (ignore `take`) | Test gap, **killed after** | The only paging test used `skip: 1, take: 1` with 2 matches, which returns 1 item even when `take` is ignored. No test limited the first page. |
| inventory-module.ts:494 (#33) | `!pageIds.length` → `false` | Equivalent | Fetching `id: []` returns no items, so the result is `[[], count]` either way. |
| inventory-module.ts:494 (#34) | early-return block → `{}` | Equivalent | Same as #33. |
| inventory-module.ts:499 (#37) | `{ id: pageIds }` → `{}` for the page fetch | Equivalent | The page is rebuilt from `pageIds` through a map, so extra rows are ignored. Only a performance difference. |
| inventory-module.ts:500 (#38) | config `{ ...config, skip, take, order }` → `{}` | Test gap, **killed after** | Dropping the caller's `select` / `relations` was not detected because the module tests only compared ids. The API depends on the requested fields being returned. |
| inventory-module.ts:531 (#57) | `join(", ")` → `join("")` in the error message | Test gap, **killed after** | The tests only passed one invalid status, so the separator never appeared in the message. |

## New or strengthened test

Commit: [3c1a11d](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/medusa/commit/3c1a11d98eb2d48eed7a56c2e90160d9b2e098ba) · Tests, all in `packages/modules/inventory/integration-tests/__tests__/inventory-module-service.spec.ts`:
- `Inventory Module Service › stock_status filter › limits the first page to take` kills #27 (inventory-module.ts:492).
- `› stock_status filter › keeps the requested relations` kills #38 (inventory-module.ts:500).
- `› stock_status filter without matching items › returns nothing when no item has the status` kills #14 and #15 (inventory-module.ts:477).
- `› stock_status filter › names every unknown stock status` kills #57 (inventory-module.ts:531).

All five show as `Killed` in the after report.

## Questions

1. **What did the surviving mutants reveal about your tests?** Most survivors (11 of 16) were equivalent. They remove shortcuts such as early returns and narrower queries that only save database work, which no test can observe through results. The five real gaps were all edge cases at the boundaries of the paging code:
   - a first page limited by `take`;
   - the case where nothing in the database has the status;
   - the caller's `relations` / `select` being passed through;
   - more than one invalid value.

   The tests checked the main behaviour (which items, in what order, how many) well. They did not check that the filter leaves the rest of the list contract (paging and requested fields) intact.

2. **Did any surviving mutant point to an assertion whose expected value was not based on the requirements?** Yes, partly. #57 is in the error message text, and the expected messages in "rejects an unknown stock status" and "names every unknown stock status" come from wording I chose in the code, not from the issue. The issue only implies that invalid input should be rejected; the HTTP test checks the requirement-level behaviour (a 400 error). The other expected values (which items are low or out of stock, the sort order, counts, an empty result) come from the acceptance criteria, the threshold rule agreed in #61, and the sort order agreed in the #62 discussion.

3. **AI use.** Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5) did the following:
   - installed and configured StrykerJS;
   - found and worked around the three setup problems above: the module tests load `dist/`, Babel drops parameter decorators (located by capturing the instrumented file during a dry run and reproducing it with Babel directly), and the `describe("")` coverage-ID mismatch;
   - wrote the module-level `stock_status` tests;
   - classified each survivor;
   - wrote the four tests that kill the gap survivors.

   What was verified:
   - The baseline run passed all tests before mutation.
   - After each Stryker run, the source file was checked to contain no instrumentation.
   - The scores in this doc were recomputed from the committed JSON reports.
   - The equivalence claims were checked by reading the code paths described in the table.

   Verified by me: I reran `npx stryker run` myself with this config, and I reviewed this whole document: the setup notes, every row of the surviving-mutants table, the new tests and the answers above. I also checked the feature manually in the admin inventory page.

# Mutation testing: Issue #112 -- Add API to create and manage product bundles

## New or strengthened test

Commit: [5dec1f5653](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/medusa/commit/5dec1f5653) · Test file: `packages/core/core-flows/src/product/utils/__tests__/bundle-edge-cases.spec.ts` (14 tests, 57 in the folder in total)

Representative tests and the mutants they kill (all are `Killed` in `-after.json`):

| Test (file › test name) | Kills |
|---|---|
| bundle-edge-cases.spec.ts › validateBundleComponents error messages › lists every duplicated variant, separated by commas | bundle.ts:120 |
| › validateBundleComponents optional fields › rejects a variant with no inventory items as a normal error | bundle.ts:155 |
| › isEmptyMetadataUpdate edge cases › is false for an object with keys | bundle.ts:279 (`&&` to `\|\|`) |
| › isEmptyMetadataUpdate edge cases › is false for non-object values | bundle.ts:279 (`typeof` forced to `true`) |
| › protectBundleUpdate marker removal › rejects an update that sets the bundle marker to undefined | bundle.ts:323 |
| › getBundleVariantId error message › reports 0 variants when the list is missing | bundle.ts:415 |

## Questions

1. **What did the surviving mutants reveal about your tests?**
   The existing 43 tests checked that the right error type was thrown, but not what the error said. Seven of the 14 gaps were list separators and variant ids inside messages (lines 120, 133, 134, 146, 257, 398, 415). These messages only ever showed a single item in the tests, so a list of several items was untested, even though acceptance criterion 11 says the error must name every bundle. The other 7 were edge cases around absent optional fields (`inventory_items`, `product`, an unloaded variant) and non-object or `undefined` metadata. The suite was good at the main paths and weak at inputs that are valid but unusual. The 6 equivalent mutants are defensive defaults and redundant checks, where no test could tell the difference.

2. **Did any surviving mutant point to an assertion whose expected value was not based on the requirements? Explain.**
   No existing assertion had a wrong expected value. The survivors came from assertions that were missing, not from assertions with incorrect values. The reverse is true of the tests I added: the separator tests expect messages such as `"A" (b1), "B" (b2)` and `a, b`. Those exact strings come from how `bundle.ts` formats its messages, not from a requirement. Requirement 11 only demands that every bundle is named, so a different separator would still meet the requirement and would fail these tests. The tests check the "every item is listed" behavior, but they also pin the comma-and-space format, which is stricter than the requirements.

3. **If you used AI to configure the tool, analyze survivors, or write tests, what did it produce and what did you verify or correct?**
   AI (Claude Code) was used for all three. It installed `@stryker-mutator/core` and `@stryker-mutator/jest-runner`, wrote `stryker.config.mjs`, classified the 20 survivors, and wrote `bundle-edge-cases.spec.ts`. What was corrected or checked along the way:
   - The first config attempt failed because Stryker's CLI cannot override nested options, so the report path is now read from the `STRYKER_JSON_REPORT` environment variable. The sandbox copy also broke the package's relative `require("../../../define_jest_config")`, so the run uses `inPlace: true`, and the temp directory sits at the repo root so Jest does not find a second copy of the tests.
   - The first mutation run was on the wrong feature: files from an uncommitted activity-log branch had been labeled as issue 112. This was caught by checking the issue 112 branch, and those reports were discarded and redone on `bundle.ts`.
   - The AI's survivor classification was checked mechanically: after adding the tests, the re-run killed 14 more mutants (183 to 197 killed), matching the 14 gaps, and left exactly the 6 mutants classified as equivalent. The 14 new tests, the `-before.json` and `-after.json` scores, and the 43 existing tests were all run, and the scores in this file were computed from the reports, not copied from the terminal.
   Overall, Claude Code did a reasonable job with the mutation testing. Other than some issues in running on the wrong files, it tremendouly sped up the setup process, where I was having inital trouble. I read through both the before and after .json reports, to make sure everything looked like it was running correctly. As for writing the new tests, I analyzed the diff as I would normally after I used Claude Code to write tests. Claude was quite sucessful, as there was a large jump in performance between the before and the after. Finally, Claude asisted in helping clarify a few things, as this was my first time mutation testing.
```

```text
     4	/**
     5	 * The export's columns, in the order the import template expects them.
     6	 */
     7	export const EXPORT_COLUMNS = Object.values(COLUMNS)
     8	
     9	/**
    10	 * Writes a rule list in the import's format, `attribute:operator:value1|value2`
    11	 * with rules separated by `;`. Rules missing an attribute, an operator or every
    12	 * value are left out, since the import can't read them back.
    13	 */
    14	const serializeRules = (rules?: PromotionRuleDTO[]): string =>
    15	  (rules ?? [])
    16	    .map((rule) => {
    17	      const values = (rule.values ?? [])
    18	        .map((ruleValue) => ruleValue.value)
    19	        .filter((value): value is string => !!value)
    20	
    21	      if (!rule.attribute || !rule.operator || !values.length) {
    22	        return undefined
    23	      }
    24	
    25	      return `${rule.attribute}:${rule.operator}:${values.join("|")}`
    26	    })
    27	    .filter(Boolean)
    28	    .join(";")
    29	
    30	/**
    31	 * Writes a value the import reads as a boolean. A promotion that has never had
    32	 * the flag set exports an empty cell rather than `false`, which the import
    33	 * treats the same way.
    34	 */
    35	const serializeBoolean = (value?: boolean): string =>
    36	  typeof value === "boolean" ? String(value) : ""
    37

    39	  typeof value === "number" ? String(value) : ""
```

_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-11-19 01:23:43Z)**_

<tool-use data-tool-type="shell" data-tool-name="Bash"><details>

```text
Closes #97

What: Adds a promotion CSV export. The Promotions list has an Export action next to Import. It opens a drawer, and confirming starts a background export of every promotion matching the list's current filters and search. The file uses the promotion import's columns, so an exported file can be imported again.

Why: Promotions could be imported but not exported, so there was no way to review them in a spreadsheet, keep a backup, or move them to another store. My spec review and the answers to the issue's open questions are on #97.

How: It follows the customer export file for file: a step that pages through promotions with an id cursor and streams the CSV to the File Module, a workflow that runs the step in the background and sends a feed notification on success or failure, `POST /admin/promotions/export` returning 202 with a transaction ID, an SDK method, and the Export action on the list.

The one deliberate difference is that the row conversion stays in `export-promotions.ts`, where the first commits on this branch put it, instead of living inside the step as the customer version does. The step imports `normalizePromotionForExport` and `EXPORT_COLUMNS` from there. The columns come from the import's own `COLUMNS` map rather than a second copy of the list, so the two can't drift when a column is added later.

Rules go out in the import's `attribute:operator:value1|value2` form, booleans as `true` and `false`, and anything the promotion doesn't have as an empty cell. A rule with no readable values is left out rather than written in a form the import would reject. The Export link carries the list's query string, which is how the drawer reads the same filters the list is showing.

## Test Evidence

| Acceptance criterion | Test(s) | Level | Source of expected value |
|---|---|---|---|
| AC1: the promotions list has an Export action next to Import | `promotion-list-table.spec.tsx > links to the promotion export from the list header` | unit | AC |
| AC2: the export covers every promotion matching the list's filters and search, not only the current page | `promotion-list-table.spec.tsx > forwards the list's filters and search to the export`; `promotion-export.spec.tsx > sends the list's current filters with the export request`; `promotion-export.spec.ts > exports only the promotions matching the search`; `> ignores pagination and exports every matching promotion` | unit, integration | AC |
| AC3: same column headers, in the same order, as the import template | `export-promotions.spec.ts > uses the import template's columns in the template's order`; `promotion-export.spec.ts > exports every promotion using the import template's columns` | unit, integration | AC. The header is a literal in both tests, written from the list in AC3, not read from the code |
| AC4: rules use `attribute:operator:value`, values joined by `\|`, rules by `;` | `export-promotions.spec.ts > joins a rule's values with \| and separate rules with ;`; `> writes the buyget quantities and both rule columns`; `promotion-export.spec.ts > writes each promotion as one row in the import's format` | unit, integration | AC. The expected string is AC4's own worked example |
| AC5: empty fields are empty cells, booleans are `true`/`false` | `export-promotions.spec.ts > flattens a promotion and its application method into one row`; `> leaves a field the promotion doesn't have as an empty cell`; `> writes a limit of 0 and a value of 0 rather than treating them as unset`; `promotion-export.spec.ts > writes each promotion as one row in the import's format` | unit, integration | AC. The integration test asserts the file's raw text, because the CSV reader coerces `false` and `10` back to a boolean and a number |
| AC6: importing an exported file recreates the promotion, checked with the existing import parser | `export-promotions.spec.ts > recreates a standard promotion with the same settings and rules`; `> recreates a buyget promotion with its quantities and both rule sets`; `> exports every promotion in the file, one row each` | unit | AC. The expected `CreatePromotionDTO` is written out by hand from the source promotion, not captured from a run |
| AC7: the export runs in the background, the route returns 202 with a `transaction_id`, and a notification carries the download link | `promotion-export.spec.ts`, in the `exportPromotions` helper every test goes through: it asserts the 202, the transaction ID, and the feed notification with the CSV's URL and `text/csv` type | integration | AC |
| AC8: unit tests for the conversion including rule formatting and the round trip, an HTTP integration test for the route and its filters, and a dashboard test for the Export action | All three: `export-promotions.spec.ts` (11 tests), `promotion-export.spec.ts` (5 tests), `promotion-export.spec.tsx` and `promotion-list-table.spec.tsx` (7 tests) | unit, integration | AC |

Not tested automatically, and why: nothing is manual-only. One gap worth naming though: I have not clicked the Export action in a running dashboard, so AC1 and AC2 are covered at the component level by the href and the request the drawer sends, not end to end in a browser.

AI-written tests: the step, workflow, route, drawer and all the tests on this branch were drafted with Claude Code. No expected value was copied from the output of code this PR adds, with one deliberate exception noted under Tech Debt. The headers and rule strings come from AC3 and AC4, the round trip's expected result is written out from the source promotion by hand, and the two exact CSV rows in the integration test were written from AC3's column order plus AC4 and AC5's formatting rules before the test was run; both matched on the first run.

Two things I had to correct. My first integration assertions expected `Automatic` to be the string `"false"` and `Discount Value` the string `"10"`, and the test failed: `csv2json` coerces those back to a boolean and a number when it reads the file, so a parsed row can never show how a value was written. The test now asserts the raw file text for AC5, which is what the criterion is actually about. Separately, the typecheck caught `useExportPromotions` taking a `query` argument it never used; it now passes it to the SDK the way `useExportCustomers` does.

To run them:

```
yarn workspace @medusajs/core-flows test -- promotion/helpers
yarn workspace @medusajs/dashboard test
yarn build, then with Postgres on 5433: cd integration-tests/http && DB_HOST=localhost DB_PORT=5433 DB_USERNAME=postgres DB_PASSWORD=postgres npx jest __tests__/promotions/ (use your own DB_PORT)
```

Already failing before this branch, unchanged by it: the 10 HTTP type mismatches are the ones in #98, and current develop has 12 because the bundles work added 2 more. The 2 skipped integration tests are `it.skip` in `promotions.spec.ts` on develop. `@medusajs/icons` fails 464 of 464 and `@medusajs/ui` 3 of 40, both from the React 19 and React 18 mismatch in #98. CI doesn't run on PRs here, so these runs stand in for it.

## Tech Debt

Introduced: a rule value containing `;`, `|` or `:` exports fine but reads back as a different rule, because the import splits on those. In practice these values are IDs and currency codes. There's a test pinning the behavior so it's documented rather than discovered, and that is the one expected value taken from existing code rather than an AC, since it records what the import parser does today. The reasoning is in my comment on #97, and fixing it means an escaping scheme on both sides, which is its own issue.

Introduced: `useExportPromotions` takes the filters as a hook argument and ignores the payload passed to `mutateAsync`, which is how `useExportCustomers` works. The drawer passes the same value to both, so it behaves correctly, but the mutation's payload type is misleading.

Encountered: `en.json` has `"duplicate": "Duplicate"` twice in the `actions` block, at lines 120 and 147. JSON parsers keep the last one, so nothing is broken, but a round trip through a JSON parser silently drops one. I hit that while adding the export keys and switched to a text insert to leave it alone. It predates this branch.

Encountered: the export is tied to the import's template by design, so a promotion field with no column can't be exported. Usage counts, campaign details and campaign budgets are the ones that come up, and the issue lists them as out of scope.

Encountered: this branch is 16 commits behind develop, including the bundles API and the low-stock dashboard. Nothing it touches overlaps, and the suites above pass, but it should take a merge from develop before it goes in.
```

````markdown
# Mutation testing: Issue #97 -- Export promotions to CSV

**PR(s):** #108
**Tool:** StrykerJS 10.1.1 with the Jest runner (`@stryker-mutator/core`, `@stryker-mutator/jest-runner`)
**Config:** [packages/core/core-flows/stryker.config.mjs](../../../packages/core/core-flows/stryker.config.mjs), adapted from njpiombino's setup for #62 ([packages/modules/inventory/stryker.config.json](../../../packages/modules/inventory/stryker.config.json)) and lefecko's root [stryker.config.mjs](../../../stryker.config.mjs) for #112. Credit to both; what I changed and why is under Setup below.
**Command:**

```
cd packages/core/core-flows
STRYKER_MUTATE="src/promotion/helpers/export-promotions.ts" \
STRYKER_TEST="src/promotion/helpers/__tests__/export-promotions.spec.ts" \
STRYKER_JSON_REPORT="../../../docs/sprint3/mutation/reports/97-angrapsas-before.json" \
node /tmp/stryker/node_modules/.bin/stryker run stryker.config.mjs
```

(`-after.json` for the re-run; nothing else changes.)

**Reports:** [before](reports/97-angrapsas-before.json) · [after](reports/97-angrapsas-after.json)
**Mutation score:** before 90.63% → after 96.88%

| | Killed | Survived | No coverage | Total | Score |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Before | 58 | 4 | 2 | 64 | 90.63% |
| After | 62 | 1 | 1 | 64 | 96.88% |

**Scope.** Mutated one file: `packages/core/core-flows/src/promotion/helpers/export-promotions.ts`, the row conversion #97 added (76 lines, 64 mutants). It is the only part of the PR that is pure functions with a plain Jest unit spec, so it needs no database and the suite runs in about 1.5 seconds. Not mutated: the step, workflow and route, which are covered by the HTTP integration suite that boots a server against built packages; and the dashboard Export action, which is Vitest, not Jest.

Tests run: `src/promotion/helpers/__tests__/export-promotions.spec.ts`, 11 tests before and 14 after. Verified by `grep` that no other test file imports `export-promotions`, `EXPORT_COLUMNS` or `normalizePromotionForExport`, so restricting the run to this one spec cannot hide a test that would have killed a mutant.

## Setup

The tests in this package run on `src/` through `@swc/jest`, not on `dist/`, so none of njpiombino's build machinery was needed: no `buildCommand`, no decorator restoration (the file has no decorators), no `concurrency: 1` (no database). What carried over from both teammates' configs is `inPlace: true` and a `tempDirName` at the repo root. Both are necessary here for the same reasons they gave: this package's `jest.config.js` does a relative `require("../../../define_jest_config")`, which breaks from a sandbox two directories deeper, and a temp directory inside the package makes Jest discover Stryker's backup copy of the tests and run everything twice.

Two things I had to work out myself:

- **Installing the tool.** `npm install --no-save` inside the repo, which lefecko used, fails here: npm tries to re-resolve the whole yarn-managed tree and hits a pre-existing rollup/vite peer conflict that has nothing to do with Stryker. I installed it into a directory outside the repo and called the binary by path, so `package.json` and `yarn.lock` are untouched.
- **Retargeting.** The file to mutate, the spec to run and the report path all come from environment variables, so pointing this at a second issue's file is three variables and no edit to the config. lefecko's config parameterises the report path the same way, because Stryker's CLI cannot override nested options.

**The `--bail` question.** This workspace's `test` script is `jest --bail --forceExit --passWithNoTests`, so I checked whether bail was hiding or faking survivors before trusting any of the numbers below. It is not, on three pieces of evidence:

1. `--bail` is a CLI flag in the `package.json` script. Stryker's jest-runner loads `jest.config.js` programmatically and never runs that script; the resolved config has no `bail` key (`'bail' in require('./jest.config.js')` is `false`).
2. Both reports record all 11 (then 14) tests, so nothing was skipped in the dry run.
3. As a control I re-ran the before run twice more, once with `bail: 1` forced into the Jest config and once with `coverageAnalysis: "all"` so every test runs against every mutant. Both produced the same 58/4/2 split and the same six non-killed mutants, mutant for mutant.

Bail could not change a verdict in any case: a mutant is killed when at least one test fails, so stopping at the first failure only ends a run whose outcome is already decided, and a survivor is a run in which nothing failed, so bail never fires.

## Surviving mutants

All six mutants that were not killed in the before run, which is every one of them (fewer than 10, so all are analysed). Line numbers are in `export-promotions.ts`; the source is byte-identical in both reports.

| Location (file:line) | Mutation | Equivalent or test gap? | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| export-promotions.ts:15 (id 3) | `(rules ?? [])` → `(rules ?? ["Stryker was here"])` | Equivalent | The fallback only runs when `rules` is nullish. The injected string has no `attribute` and no `values`, so the guard on line 21 drops it and the column joins to `""`, exactly as an empty array does. No observable difference. |
| export-promotions.ts:17 (id 7) | `(rule.values ?? [])` → `["Stryker was here"]` | Equivalent | Same shape: `"Stryker was here".value` is `undefined`, the filter on line 19 removes it, `values` is empty and the rule is dropped. Reported as no coverage because `values` is required in `PromotionRuleDTO` and the step selects `rules.values.value`, so the fallback is defensive and nothing reaches it. |
| export-promotions.ts:17 (id 5) | drops `.filter((value): value is string => !!value)` | **Test gap, killed after** | `PromotionRuleValueDTO.value` is optional, so a rule value row with no value is valid input. The one existing test for an unreadable rule passes `values: []`, so the filter never ran on a non-empty list. With the mutant a blank value is kept and the rule exports as `attribute:operator:`, which the import rejects. |
| export-promotions.ts:21 (id 15) | `!rule.attribute \|\| !rule.operator` → `false` | **Test gap, killed after** | Removes both guards. A rule missing its attribute or its operator would be written out as `undefined:eq:eur`. No test had a rule missing either field. |
| export-promotions.ts:21 (id 16) | `\|\|` → `&&` between the attribute and operator guards | **Test gap, killed after** | A rule is then dropped only when *both* fields are missing, so a rule missing just one of them is exported. Same untested input as id 15. |
| export-promotions.ts:53 (id 39) | `promotion.code ?? ""` → `?? "Stryker was here!"` | **Test gap, killed after** | `PromotionDTO.code` is optional, so the fallback is reachable, but every promotion in the suite had a code: the "empty cell" test asserts every other column while setting `code: "BARE"`. Low value in practice, since the `code` column is non-nullable in the database, but AC5 covers it and the branch was untested. |

The four gaps are one finding. The function's own contract, in the comment above `serializeRules`, is that a rule missing an attribute, an operator or every value is left out because the import cannot read it back. Only the third of those three was tested. That matters more than a missing assertion: the import's `parseRules` rejects the *whole* rules column when a rule has a blank attribute, an unknown operator or no values, so one incompletely written rule does not degrade gracefully, it makes the entire file fail to import and breaks AC6.

After the re-run the two remaining non-killed mutants are exactly the two classified as equivalent, with no previously killed mutant regressing (checked by diffing the two reports on mutant id, not on line number: ids 13 and 15 are both `ConditionalExpression → "false"` on line 21 and only differ by sub-expression).

## New or strengthened test

Not committed on this branch. The three tests belong in the #97 PR's own spec, so they are handed over as `~/csci535-notes/sprint3-97-mutation-tests.patch` for `feat/issue-97-export-promotions-csv`; the after report here was produced with them applied.

Test file: `packages/core/core-flows/src/promotion/helpers/__tests__/export-promotions.spec.ts`

| Test (file › test name) | Kills |
|---|---|
| export-promotions.spec.ts › exported promotions read back through the import › leaves out a rule with no attribute or no operator, so the file still imports | ids 15 and 16 (line 21) |
| › exported promotions read back through the import › leaves out a rule whose only value is blank, so the file still imports | id 5 (line 17) |
| › normalizePromotionForExport › leaves the code cell empty for a promotion that has no code | id 39 (line 53) |

All four show as `Killed` in the after report.

The two rule tests assert the round trip (`errors` is empty and the promotion comes back with the rules that were readable) rather than the exported string. That is AC6's own wording, and it is also the stricter check: it fails for any malformed rule the export emits, whatever formatting the code happens to use.

## Questions

**1. What did the surviving mutants reveal about your tests?**

That the suite tested the function's documented behaviour asymmetrically. `serializeRules` promises to leave out a rule missing an attribute, an operator or every value, and the spec covered only the missing-values case, which is also the easiest to construct. The two mutants on line 21 survived because both the attribute guard and the operator guard were dead weight as far as the tests were concerned, and a mutant could delete them silently. The same for the blank-value filter on line 17, which never ran on a non-empty list because the one unreadable-rule test passed `values: []` and so short-circuited on length instead.

The pattern is that the tests were built from whole, well-formed promotions, with absence modelled as a whole field or a whole list being missing, never as a partly-filled nested object. That is the shape the export actually has to defend against, because the step selects nested rule fields individually and gets back whatever the database holds. The 58 mutants killed on the first run show the main paths and the formatting were covered properly; the gaps were all one level down, inside the rule objects.

The two equivalent survivors are both `?? []` defaults, where the injected array is dropped by the same validation that drops a real unreadable rule. Nothing can distinguish them through the function's output, which is the signature of a guard that exists for safety rather than for behaviour.

**2. Did any surviving mutant point to an assertion whose expected value was not based on the requirements?**

Not among the existing assertions: the gaps were assertions that did not exist, not assertions with wrong expected values. The existing expected values hold up. The header in the "columns in the template's order" test is a literal written from AC3 rather than read from `COLUMNS`, which is why the `StringLiteral` mutants in the column keys all died, and the round-trip tests write out the expected `CreatePromotionDTO` by hand from the source promotion.

The one place worth naming is the test I wrote for id 39. Asserting `row.Code === ""` does pin the empty string, which is a formatting choice, though AC5 states it directly ("anything the promotion doesn't have is an empty cell"), so the expected value traces to a criterion. I deliberately avoided the same shape for the two rule tests: asserting the exported string `"currency_code:eq:eur"` would have killed the same mutants while pinning the export's formatting, so instead they assert that the file imports back with no errors and the right rules, which is what AC6 asks for and does not depend on how the rule is spelled. That distinction is the thing I would not have thought about without the survivors: the stricter-looking string assertion is the weaker test, because it passes for a file no one can import.

A related limitation, recorded as tech debt on #97 and not something mutation testing surfaced: the existing test "does not round trip a rule value containing a delimiter" takes its expected value from what the import parser does today, not from a requirement. It pins known-wrong behaviour on purpose.

**3. If you used AI to configure the tool, analyze survivors, or write tests, what did it produce and what did you verify or correct?**

Claude Code (Opus 5) set up and ran the tool, classified the six survivors and drafted the three tests. It produced the config, worked out the install problem, and ran the controls described under Setup.

What I checked:

- The dry run passed all 11 tests before any mutation, and the source file contains no leftover instrumentation after each run.
- The `--bail` claim was not taken on reasoning. The two control runs, with bail forced on and with `coverageAnalysis: "all"`, are what settles it, and they agree with the committed before run mutant for mutant.
- The classifications were checked mechanically as well as by reading: the re-run killed exactly the four mutants classified as gaps and left exactly the two classified as equivalent, with no regressions. If a classification had been wrong, that count would not have matched.
- The scores and counts in this document were recomputed from the committed JSON reports rather than copied from the terminal.
- The report diff was redone keyed on mutant id after the first attempt keyed on line and column, which collapsed two distinct `ConditionalExpression` mutants on line 21 and produced a misleading list of which tests killed what.
- One correction worth recording: the first version of the rule tests asserted the exported strings. That would have killed the same mutants, but it pins formatting the requirements do not specify, so the tests were rewritten to assert the round trip instead. The reasoning is in question 2.
````

## The --bail question

It is not hiding or faking anything, on three pieces of evidence. `--bail` is a CLI flag in the package's `test` script; Stryker's jest-runner loads `jest.config.js` programmatically and never runs that script, and the resolved config has no `bail` key. Both reports record all 11 tests. And as a control I re-ran the before run twice, once with `bail: 1` forced into the Jest config and once with `coverageAnalysis: "all"`, and both gave the same six non-killed mutants, mutant for mutant.

Separately, I grepped to confirm nothing outside that one spec imports the file, so narrowing the test set can't produce false survivors either.

## Survivors

Six, all analysed. Two are equivalent (`?? []` defaults where the injected array gets dropped by the same validation). Four were real gaps, and they're one finding: `serializeRules` documents that a rule missing an attribute, an operator or every value is left out, and only the missing-values third was tested. That matters more than a missing assertion, because the import's `parseRules` rejects the *whole* rules column on one malformed rule, so the file stops importing entirely and AC6 breaks.

## The test, for you to apply

Not committed here. Three tests, handed over as `~/csci535-notes/sprint3-97-mutation-tests.patch`, verified to apply cleanly to `feat/issue-97-export-promotions-csv`:

They kill all four gap mutants, zero regressions. Two of them assert the round trip (`errors` empty, rules come back) rather than the exported string. My first draft asserted the strings, which kills the same mutants but pins formatting no AC specifies. The round-trip version is grounded in AC6 and is the stricter test, since it fails for any malformed rule whatever the formatting.

A different Jest package needs the file copied there; the dashboard would need the Vitest runner instead.

**I leaned on lefecko's config more than njpiombino's, deliberately.** You pointed me at njpiombino's, but his setup is built around problems core-flows doesn't have: his module tests load `dist/`, so he needs a rebuild step and a Babel decorator workaround, plus `concurrency: 1` for the shared test database. Core-flows tests run on `src/` through `@swc/jest`, so none of that applies. lefecko's config already targets this exact package and is parameterised for retargeting, which is what you asked for. I kept `inPlace` and the root `tempDirName` from both, credited both in the doc, and wrote up what I changed and why.

**The Stryker install is in the session scratchpad and will be wiped.** `npm install --no-save` inside the repo fails here (npm tries to re-resolve the yarn tree and hits a pre-existing rollup/vite peer conflict, nothing to do with Stryker), which is why lefecko's documented install command won't work as written. For reruns, install it somewhere durable like `/tmp/stryker` as the config header documents.
